The Insular vole, Microtus abbreviatus, is a small arvicoline rodent endemic to the islands of the Bering Sea, and its life-history parameters have been estimated primarily through captive studies. Newborn pups emerge altricial and naked, with a recorded wet weight at birth of approximately 3.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.5 grams], placing them on the smaller end of the range for the genus. This modest neonatal mass is coupled with rapid early development, likely an adaptation to the short, cold summers characteristic of its maritime tundra habitat. A gestation period of about 21 days [tg = about 21 days] has been reported for Microtus abbreviatus at a stable body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], a value inferred from its congener Microtus arvalis and consistent with the compact gestation typical of arvicoline rodents breeding under cool maritime conditions. The relatively brief gestation facilitates a high potential for rapid population turnover. Following birth, the suckling juveniles remain in the natal nest, entirely dependent on maternal milk, and the weaning process begins as they transition to solid vegetation.

The transition to nutritional independence marks a critical threshold in the early life of Microtus abbreviatus. Under the same thermoneutral conditions of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the weaning period is completed approximately 20 days after birth [tx = approximately 20 days after birth], an interval during which the young must develop the digestive capabilities necessary to process fibrous plant material. This relatively early weaning age enables females to return rapidly to breeding condition. The post-weaning period is one of intense somatic growth, as the young voles must accumulate sufficient body mass and fat reserves to survive their first winter. After weaning, the juvenile individuals enter a phase of rapid mass gain, feeding heavily on grasses and sedges to build their body size. The ultimate wet weight for adult females in this population is observed to plateau at around 60 grams [Wwi = around 60 grams], a figure consistent with the lower range observed among Microtus species, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by the species' marginal island habitat and short growing season.

Sexual maturation in the Insular vole proceeds on a timetable that reflects the constraints of its short growing season. Females attain puberty at a remarkably consistent age, reaching sexual maturity approximately 38 days after birth [tp = approximately 38 days after birth], a figure derived from studies on Microtus arvalis and applicable under captive conditions at 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This rapid maturation is a hallmark of many Microtus species, allowing them to breed within the same season in which they are born. Consequently, populations can exhibit exponential growth when environmental conditions are favorable. The onset of gonadal activity is closely tied to photoperiod and nutritional status, with well-fed females often reaching first estrus sooner than those on restricted diets. This early puberty contributes significantly to the high intrinsic rate of increase that characterizes the species. Furthermore, the ability to produce multiple litters across the summer is a key demographic strategy.

Reproductive output in Microtus abbreviatus is defined by a combination of moderate litter sizes and a compressed breeding season. Females typically produce 5.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5.5 pups per litter], a fecundity that is supplemented by the capacity to produce multiple litters during the active summer months. Under conditions approximating a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the maximum reproductive potential is meaningfully expressed in terms of seasonal productivity. For instance, if a female produces approximately 5.1 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 5.1 litters per year], her total yearly fecundity can exceed 28 pups, demonstrating a high reproductive potential that allows populations to recover quickly from low densities. This strategy is typical of r-selected species inhabiting unpredictable environments.

Longevity data for the Insular vole remain limited, but comparative studies from related species provide useful estimates for its life span. Based on records from Microtus arvalis, the maximum lifespan for Microtus abbreviatus is projected to be around 4.8 years [am = around 4.8 years] under optimal conditions at 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. In the wild, however, this value is rarely attained due to intense predation pressure from avian and mammalian predators, as well as the harshness of the winter environment. Most individuals likely survive for only one or two breeding seasons, a pattern common among small mammals exhibiting high reproductive turnover. The existence of two distinct values for asymptotic body mass — 60 grams [Wwi = 60 grams] for females and a larger 90 grams [Wwi = 90 grams] for males — mirrors the moderate sexual size dimorphism reported for Microtus arvalis and other microtine rodents, where males typically achieve 20 to 30 percent greater body mass to support territorial defense and mate searching during the breeding season.
